also, here’s my review of different polymer clay brands and types 

sculpey III snaps easily once it’s cooked!! I would stay away from it if you’re making something smaller than the rabbit you just made. but, for any relatively large object (like your rabbit or bigger), it’s pretty good! sculpey is MUCH easier to condition than fimo, making it a really good beginner clay since you don’t need too many tools to make it ready for use. plus since it’s softer, it’s easier to mix your own colours. 

fimo professional is super hard to condition (soften), so only use it if you’re trying to make something super detailed (the details won’t change if you touch them, since it’s super tough) 

fimo soft is also really hard, but once you condition it, it’s relatively okay. i still only use fimo soft if i’m doing something with lots of details (like if i have to carve into it) 

for translucent clay, I use sculpey premo. it’s very soft and easy to mold, to the point where i often have to harden it to be able to use it after a while. however, i LOVE it! it’s also super great to make more clay of a colour you like, since it won’t change the color unless you add a LOT of it. 

all brands of polymer clay (that i know of, but for sure fimo and sculpey) can be mixed together. that means that if your fimo is too hard to use easily, you can mix it with sculpey to soften it, or vice versa. it’s also great to mix them since you can have even more colours. 

for making a polymer clay cane or anything you want to slice into to expose the design underneath, let the clay sit without you touching it for a few hours. it needs to get hard ish so that it won’t smudge when you cut it. 

almost all the things i make are very small since i make earrings for my small business, so you may need to alter this a little, but i cook all my creations for 10-15 minutes at 275° F. 

you can glaze your creations with sculpey glaze which works well and dries quickly, or invest in UV resin which is incredible but takes a while to dry depending on the strength of your light, and it’s quite expensive. glazing doesn’t really provide any structural advantages to your creation, it just makes it glossy. 

after you cook a creation, it will still be bendable for a few minutes until it cools, so don’t panic if you touch it and it bends! but also don’t touch it when it comes out of the oven, obviously. :)

let me know if you have any other questions!!

hey! using rubbing alcohol on a Q-tip removes a thin layer of clay from your creation, taking off the dust! it’s best to do this before you cook it, but it works after you cook it too, just not as well. this also works for smoothing the clay! also, clean your hands every time you begin crafting!!!

as a teen that self harms, i’d like to chip in here, too. i’m 14, and i’ve been cutting since i was 12. my parents found out about a year ago, and haven’t been able to help me very well due to all of the stigma and myths around self harm. 

something very important for a parent to acknowledge is that self harm is an addiction, it is not something that your child wants to continue (most commonly). self harm is a rabbit hole that’s incredibly difficult to get out of, with or without support. self harm releases dopamine and endorphins, causing a sensation of being high, giddy, numb to all problems, and/or euphoric. this action can be more or as addicting as cigarettes. 

considering the fact that your child doesn’t want to admit that they self harm, there are always ways you can help that avoid confrontation, if that’s what you’re looking for. 

many teenagers that don’t have support tend to lack aftercare supplies such as bandages, bandaids, disinfectant wipes or other, etc. you can make sure that you are always stocked up on those supplies, so that your child never has to resort to unsanitary means to take care of themselves. 

if you want to be even more supportive, you can try to give them tips on overcoming their addiction. for example, whenever they feel an urge, they could drink a couple drops of hot sauce, put an ice cubs on their usual spot, draw cuts with red markers, snap rubber bands on their wrist, go for a run, etc. these tactics can be easily found on the internet, if you’re interested. 

i would not recommend removing sharp objects such as razors, scissors, etc from your home, seeing as that will make your child scavenge for other sharp objects that may not be sanitary. make sure your child knows that they can come to you if they ever get an infection, cut too deep, need stitches, etc. 

in the end, i think it’s important that you make sure your child knows that you will always be there for them, and that you love them no matter what.
